questions.stem: The GOVERNOR of a State is APPOINTED by:

options.option_text: The Chief Minister of the State
The PRESIDENT OF INDIA (Article 155) — under warrant under his hand + seal, usually on advice of the Union government

questions.explanation: GOVERNOR of a STATE — Executive head of a State; titular / ceremonial counterpart of the President at state level. APPOINTMENT: ARTICLE 155 — appointed by the PRESIDENT (on the advice of Prime Minister / Union Govt). PROCESS: President issues a warrant (sign + seal) of appointment. Not elected. QUALIFICATIONS: Art 157 — (1) CITIZEN of India; (2) aged 35 YEARS or more; (3) must NOT hold any office of profit; (4) NOT member of either House of Parliament / State Legislature (if he/she is, must resign before assuming office). CONVENTIONS (not binding): (a) Governor should NOT be from the state he/she governs (to ensure impartiality); (b) CM's opinion 'should' be consulted — not binding. OATH (Art 159) — administered by the CHIEF JUSTICE OF the State's HIGH COURT (or senior-most HC judge if CJ unavailable). TERM (Art 156): 5 years, holds office at the pleasure of the President — meaning President can dismiss anytime (political instrument of Centre). Can resign by writing to the President. Can be re-appointed. Same person can be Governor of 2 or more states (Art 153 post-7th CAA 1956). REMUNERATION: Rs 3.5 lakh/month (as of 2018) + free accommodation (RAJ BHAVAN) + medical + allowances. PRIVILEGES: parliamentary + civil immunity for official acts (Art 361) — cannot be called to court during tenure for personal acts; civil proceedings only after 2-month notice. CURRENT (2026): varying by state. CAUTION: Governors have been politically controversial — accused of being 'extended arm of Centre' (Bommai case 1994 + recent WB-Bihar-Kerala-TN standoffs on Bill assent delays).
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: The Governor is called the 'EXTENDED ARM OF THE CENTRE' because:

options.option_text: He is APPOINTED by + holds office at the PLEASURE of the PRESIDENT (i.e., Centre); performs DUAL role — representative of Centre + constitutional head of state
He directly serves the Home Minister
He is appointed by the Governor General

questions.explanation: GOVERNOR — DUAL CAPACITY: (1) CONSTITUTIONAL HEAD of the STATE (analogous to President at centre); (2) REPRESENTATIVE of the CENTRE / UNION GOVERNMENT. This dual role is built into the Constitution + has been a flashpoint of centre-state tensions. 'EXTENDED ARM of the CENTRE' — phrase arises because: (a) APPOINTMENT + REMOVAL by President (practically by Central ruling party); no fixed term, holds office at 'pleasure of the President' (Art 156); (b) Governor reserves Bills for Presidential consideration (Art 200 + 201) — particularly contentious; (c) Governor recommends PRESIDENT'S RULE (Art 356) to the President — misused historically (e.g., pre-1994 — struck down S.R. Bommai case); (d) acts on 'DISCRETIONARY' powers beyond ministerial advice (Art 163); sometimes guided by Centre. CRITICISMS (Sarkaria Commission 1988, Punchhi Commission 2010, ARC-II reports): (a) partisan appointees — often retired politicians from ruling party — Justice V.R. Krishna Iyer called them 'LACKEYS' of ruling party; (b) dismissed when Centre changes — 8 governors dismissed 1989 (V.P. Singh), 4 in 2004 (UPA), multiple in 2014 (NDA); (c) undue delays in assenting to State Bills (e.g., 2023 Tamil Nadu Governor RN Ravi + Kerala Governor Arif Mohammed Khan controversies — SC rulings on Bill assent timelines, Nov 2023 + April 2024). RECOMMENDATIONS for REFORM: (a) ELIMINATE 'pleasure' tenure, fix 5-year term; (b) appointment on consultation with state CM (NCRWC 2002 — mandatory); (c) non-politician persons of eminence; (d) timeline for Bill assent. NONE fully implemented. SC rulings: Nabam Rebia (Arunachal 2016) — Governor should not become a power unto himself. Rameshwar Prasad (Bihar 2005) — Governor's Report on imposition of Art 356 subject to judicial review.
questions.subject: Polity

options.option_text: Appointing CM in hung legislatures; reserving Bills for President's consideration; recommending President's Rule — constitutional + situational discretion

questions.explanation: GOVERNOR's DISCRETIONARY POWERS — Art 163(1) + (2). NOT OBLIGATED to act on CM's advice in these cases. TYPES: (1) CONSTITUTIONAL DISCRETION — explicit in Constitution: (a) RESERVATION of BILLS passed by State Legislature for consideration of the President (Art 200-201) — e.g., Bills affecting HC powers, compulsory Bills, derogation from Constitution. (b) RECOMMEND IMPOSITION OF PRESIDENT'S RULE (Art 356 + Governor's Report). (c) SEEKING information from CM about administration of state affairs (Art 167). (d) Special responsibilities regarding SCHEDULED AREAS + TRIBAL AREAS (5th Schedule — Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand; 6th Schedule — Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram). (e) Governor of ASSAM — discretion re: Tribal Belt, Hill Areas (para 12 of 6th Schedule). (f) Special: NAGALAND (Art 371A), SIKKIM (Art 371F), ARUNACHAL PRADESH etc. (2) SITUATIONAL DISCRETION — not explicit but needed in certain political situations: (a) APPOINTMENT of CHIEF MINISTER in a HUNG ASSEMBLY (no clear majority). E.g., 2017 Goa Congress-BJP tussle, 2018 Karnataka, 2022 Maharashtra. (b) DISMISSING state CoM when it loses confidence + refuses to resign. (c) DISSOLVING State Legislative Assembly on losing majority / advising alternative government. CASE LAW: (1) S.R. BOMMAI v. UoI (1994) — 9-judge SC bench; Art 356 subject to judicial review; floor test must be in assembly, not Raj Bhavan. (2) NABAM REBIA v. Deputy Speaker (Arunachal 2016) — unanimous SC ruling — Governor cannot decide whether to convene/prorogue House or advance assembly session without CoM advice. (3) RAMESHWAR PRASAD v. UoI (2005) — Bihar — Governor Buta Singh's report on Art 356 quashed. (4) SHAMSHER SINGH v. State of Punjab (1974) — reaffirmed Governor bound by CoM advice except for limited discretion. Governors have become increasingly controversial post-2019 in several BJP-opposition ruling states.

questions.stem: When a Bill passed by a State Legislature is sent to the Governor, he can:

options.option_text: FOUR options (Art 200) — assent; withhold assent; return for reconsideration (except money bills); reserve for President's consideration

questions.explanation: Article 200 — Governor's powers when a Bill is presented for assent: (1) ASSENT — signs, becomes law. (2) WITHHOLD ASSENT — 'absolute veto' (rare; rarely justifiable for ordinary bills). (3) RETURN the Bill (if NOT a Money Bill) for RECONSIDERATION with a message suggesting amendments; 'suspensive veto' — if the state legislature re-passes (with or without amendments), the Governor MUST give assent. No re-return. (4) RESERVE the Bill for the PRESIDENT's consideration (mandatory in certain cases, e.g., Bills affecting HC powers; derogatory to Constitution; land acquisition compensation below a level). KEY ISSUE: the Constitution does NOT specify a TIME LIMIT within which the Governor must decide — led to unconstitutional DELAYS in bill clearance (years in some cases — TN, Kerala, Telangana). SC INTERVENTION: (a) State of Telangana v. Governor (2023) — SC said delay cannot be indefinite. (b) State of Punjab v. Governor (Nov 2023) — 'Governor is not unelected authority above elected legislature'; must decide in reasonable time. (c) State of Kerala v. Governor + State of Tamil Nadu v. Governor RN Ravi (Apr 2024) — SC issued DIRECTIONS with timelines for Governor to act on state Bills. PROSPECTIVE OVERRULING + constitutional guidelines. ART 201 — once reserved for President, President can: give assent; withhold; direct Governor to return for reconsideration; if re-passed, President can still sit on it (no time limit in Constitution). MONEY BILLS in states (Art 207-209) — originate in Legislative Assembly only; Governor's options on a Money Bill = assent OR withhold (cannot return for reconsideration); can reserve in principle but never done on money bills. RECENT CONTROVERSIES: NEET state bills, anti-conversion bills, online gaming bills — Governors sat on them for months/years.

questions.stem: Which of the following ARTICLES deals with the APPOINTMENT of the Chief Minister + Council of Ministers of a State by the Governor?

options.option_text: ARTICLE 164 — CM appointed by Governor; other ministers on advice of CM; CoM collectively responsible to Legislative Assembly

questions.explanation: ARTICLE 164 — STATE COUNCIL OF MINISTERS. (1) CM appointed by the GOVERNOR (constitutional convention: leader of majority party in Legislative Assembly). (2) Other Ministers appointed by Governor on the advice of the CM. (3) Ministers hold office during 'pleasure' of Governor (in practice, until CM's confidence holds). (4) CoM collectively responsible to LEGISLATIVE ASSEMBLY (Art 164(2)) — must resign if loses floor test. (5) 91st CAA 2003 — State CoM size (including CM) capped at 15% of Legislative Assembly strength; minimum 12 (for small states). (6) Ministers must be members of either House within 6 MONTHS (Art 164(4)) similar to Art 75(5). (7) Salary + allowances per Legislature. Special positions: SCs/STs welfare minister mandatory in some states (Art 164(1), now covers Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, MP, Odisha post-changes). Tribal Welfare Minister (Chhattisgarh + Jharkhand); Tribal + SC + OBC Welfare (MP + Odisha). Related Articles: (a) Art 163 — CoM to AID + ADVISE Governor, except in discretionary matters; Art 163(2) — question whether matter is discretionary is finally determined by Governor (not judicially reviewable on merits, but existence subject to judicial review — Shamsher Singh + Samsher Singh). (b) Art 165 — Advocate-General of State (analog of Attorney-General). (c) Art 166 — conduct of business of Govt of State (in Governor's name); Business Rules made by Governor. (d) Art 167 — CM's duties to Governor — communicate decisions, furnish info, submit matters. COMPARISON with Centre: Art 74 (CoM to aid President), Art 75 (appointment/tenure), Art 76 (AG), Art 77 (conduct of business), Art 78 (PM's duties). State articles roughly parallel.

questions.stem: The VERY FIRST WOMAN to be APPOINTED as GOVERNOR of an Indian state was:

options.option_text: SAROJINI NAIDU (Governor of United Provinces / UP, 1947-49) — 'Nightingale of India'; poet + freedom fighter

questions.explanation: SAROJINI NAIDU (1879-1949) — 'NIGHTINGALE OF INDIA' (Bharat Kokila); poet, freedom fighter, first WOMAN PRESIDENT of INC (Kanpur session 1925, first Indian woman), first WOMAN GOVERNOR of a state (United Provinces, now UP, from 15 Aug 1947 till her death 2 March 1949). BIRTH: 13 February 1879 in HYDERABAD. WOMEN'S DAY in INDIA is her birth anniversary (13 Feb, National Women's Day). Educated Madras, Girton College Cambridge, King's College London. POETRY: Published first collection 'The Golden Threshold' (1905), later 'The Bird of Time' (1912), 'The Broken Wing' (1917). Praised by Gosse + Edmund Blunden. NATIONALIST: joined INC ~1904; close to Gandhi + Gokhale. Led women's delegation to Montagu 1917. Signed Non-Cooperation (1920), Salt Satyagraha (1930), Quit India (1942) — jailed multiple times. LEGACY: Sarojini Naidu College for Women, Hyderabad; Sarojini Nagar (Delhi + Lucknow); Marine Drive (Cuffe Parade, Mumbai) — 'Queen's Necklace' officially Netaji Subhash Chandra Bose Road. OTHER WOMEN FIRSTS: (1) first FEMALE PM = INDIRA GANDHI (1966). (2) first FEMALE PRESIDENT = PRATIBHA PATIL (2007-12); second = DROUPADI MURMU (2022-present). (3) first FEMALE CM = SUCHETA KRIPALANI (UP, 1963-67). (4) first FEMALE SUPREME COURT JUDGE = Justice M. FATHIMA BEEVI (1989). (5) first FEMALE IPS = Kiran Bedi (1972). (6) first FEMALE IAS = Anna Rajam Malhotra (1950). (7) first FEMALE FOREIGN SECRETARY = Chokila Iyer (2001). (8) first Indian WOMAN in SPACE = KALPANA CHAWLA (NASA, 1997; died 2003 Columbia disaster); Sunita Williams followed (2006, 2012, 2024-25 ISS stay). (9) first FEMALE SPEAKER of Lok Sabha = MEIRA KUMAR (2009-14). Notable Governors: LAKSHMI SAHGAL (INA); VIJAYA LAKSHMI PANDIT (Maharashtra 1962-64, 1st woman UN GA President 1953). INDIRA GANDHI famously Delhi University student + women's representative.

questions.stem: The S.R. BOMMAI v. UNION OF INDIA (1994) landmark Supreme Court judgment was primarily about:

options.option_text: Limits on MISUSE of ARTICLE 356 (President's Rule); made proclamation JUDICIALLY REVIEWABLE; floor test must be in Assembly, not Raj Bhavan

questions.explanation: S.R. BOMMAI v. UNION OF INDIA (1994) 3 SCC 1 — seminal 9-judge SC bench decision (7-2). BACKGROUND: S.R. Bommai, CM of Karnataka (1988-89), was ousted when Governor P. Venkatasubbaiah imposed Art 356 on 21 April 1989, without giving Bommai a chance to prove majority on the floor. Similar Art 356 impositions followed (Meghalaya, Nagaland, Karnataka, MP, Rajasthan, HP) — several reversed judicially. SC's KEY HOLDINGS: (1) Art 356 IS JUSTICIABLE / SUBJECT TO JUDICIAL REVIEW — Governor's report + Presidential proclamation can be struck down by SC. (2) FLOOR TEST must be held in the Legislative Assembly, NOT by the Governor in Raj Bhavan. The question of whether CM enjoys majority can ONLY be decided by Assembly. (3) If proclamation is struck down, SC can REVIVE the dismissed government + Legislative Assembly (strong remedy); can order fresh elections if feasible. (4) SECULARISM is a BASIC FEATURE of the Constitution — its violation by state government can be grounds for Art 356 (important ruling post-Babri, 1992 — Art 356 imposed on BJP-ruled UP, MP, Rajasthan, HP after Dec 1992; SC upheld). (5) Proclamation must be based on relevant material; BONA FIDE + not malafide. (6) Within 2 MONTHS proclamation must be approved by BOTH Houses of Parliament (simple majority); can be for 6 months at a time, max 3 years. (7) Till Parliamentary approval, NO irreversible action (like dissolving Assembly) should be taken — or if dissolved, can be revived. IMPACT: Art 356 impositions DRASTICALLY REDUCED post-Bommai (pre-1994 ~100+ impositions; post-1994 ~30). Cases reversed: Uttarakhand 2016, Arunachal 2016. Bommai is part of the 'basic features' + 'federalism' canon of Indian constitutional law; along with Kesavananda Bharati (1973), Maneka Gandhi (1978), Minerva Mills (1980), I.R. Coelho (2007), K.S. Puttaswamy (2017), it forms top SC rulings. PM RAO + Home Minister S.B. Chavan had imposed Art 356 in 1992 on BJP states. Sarkaria Commission (1988) recommendations largely vindicated by Bommai.

questions.stem: The Governor does NOT have which of the following powers?

options.option_text: Legislative power to summon/prorogue/dissolve Legislative Assembly
JUDICIAL power to pardon death sentences under Article 161 (limited — CANNOT pardon death; can commute/reprieve/respite)
Financial power to recommend money bills

questions.explanation: GOVERNOR's PARDONING POWER — Art 161 — LIMITED compared to President's pardoning power (Art 72). (1) GOVERNOR CAN (Art 161): grant PARDONS (except death sentence), REPRIEVES (stay), RESPITES, REMISSIONS of punishment; COMMUTE sentences (including DEATH sentences). So Governor CAN commute a DEATH SENTENCE to life, but CANNOT completely pardon/absolve a DEATH sentence (only President can). (2) Scope: limited to offences against laws to which the EXECUTIVE POWER OF THE STATE EXTENDS. Cannot pardon court-martial offences. (3) PRESIDENT can PARDON a death sentence — Art 72(1)(c). GOVERNOR'S OTHER POWERS: (1) EXECUTIVE (Art 154-155): all executive actions in Governor's name; appointment of Advocate-General, State Election Commissioner, State Public Service Commission chairman + members, Vice-Chancellors of some universities, etc. (2) LEGISLATIVE (Art 168): part of State Legislature; summons + prorogues + dissolves Assembly; gives message to Legislature; Ordinances (Art 213 — when Legislature not in session); nomination of MLCs (Art 171 — 1/6 of Legislative Council from literature, science, art, co-operative movement, social service). Can't be MLA/MLC/MP concurrently. (3) FINANCIAL (Art 202-203): annual state budget laid on his recommendation; MONEY BILLS (Art 207) can be introduced only on Governor's recommendation. Governor's approval needed for supplementary grants. (4) JUDICIAL: Art 161 pardoning power; Art 217 — CJ of SC consulted for appointment of HC judges (collegium system). (5) DIPLOMATIC / MILITARY: NONE (these are exclusively President/Centre). Special discretionary powers for Governors of NE states, Schedule 5/6 areas. COMPARING Art 72 (President) vs Art 161 (Governor): pardon death sentence = only President; pardon court-martial = only President; both = pardon, reprieve, respite, remission, commutation.

questions.stem: The same person can be appointed as GOVERNOR of TWO OR MORE STATES per:

options.option_text: Art 153 (first proviso, added by 7th CAA 1956) — allows a Governor of one state to concurrently hold charge of another state (e.g., small NE states often share a Governor)

questions.explanation: ARTICLE 153 (first proviso) — 'Nothing in this article shall prevent the appointment of the SAME person as Governor for TWO OR MORE STATES'. Added by the 7TH CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT ACT, 1956 (which also introduced the States Reorganisation on linguistic lines). RATIONALE: for efficiency + to manage small states / UTs that don't warrant separate full-time governors. EXAMPLES (historically + currently): (1) Small NORTHEASTERN STATES often share a Governor — Mizoram + Arunachal Pradesh + Nagaland at different times have had common Governors. (2) GOA + TELANGANA have shared Governors in recent years. (3) ASSAM Governor is also Governor of Meghalaya during transitional phases. UNION TERRITORIES: have ADMINISTRATORS (not Governors) except Delhi + Puducherry + J&K which have Lieutenant Governors — the LT GOVERNOR (LG) of DELHI + J&K + PUDUCHERRY differ from state Governors in specifics. LG of DELHI = most politically contentious (2015 onwards Kejriwal vs LG disputes; ultimately SC ruled in 2023 that except for land, police + public order, elected govt has executive authority; Centre countered via Govt of NCT of Delhi Amendment Act 2023 — raging dispute). LGs of UTs = Andaman + Nicobar, Puducherry, Chandigarh (same as Punjab Governor ex-officio), Dadra + Nagar Haveli + Daman + Diu, Lakshadweep. Each Administrator appointed by President. TERM: no fixed; 'pleasure of the President'. Note: GOVERNORS of STATES have charge; LIEUTENANT GOVERNORS of UTs + Administrators have charge on behalf of President. OATH: for Governor = from State HC CJ; for LG = from same or Central authorities. SALARY + allowances for Governor/LG is charged upon CONSOLIDATED FUND of INDIA (not State) — Art 158(3) — so State Legislature cannot debate/vote reduction.

questions.stem: The SARKARIA COMMISSION (1988) + the PUNCHHI COMMISSION (2010) both studied + recommended reforms on:

options.option_text: CENTRE-STATE relations; including Governor's role, Art 356, Inter-State Council, residuary powers, legislative + administrative relations

questions.explanation: SARKARIA + PUNCHHI COMMISSIONS on CENTRE-STATE RELATIONS: (1) SARKARIA COMMISSION (1983-1988) — chaired by JUSTICE R.S. SARKARIA (retired SC judge). Set up by Indira Gandhi govt 1983 during federal tensions (Punjab, AP, Assam movements). Submitted REPORT in JANUARY 1988 to PM RAJIV GANDHI. Comprehensive 19-chapter review. KEY RECOMMENDATIONS: (a) Strong Centre but decentralisation where possible; (b) RESIDUARY POWERS (Art 248) — concurrent rather than Union-only (not accepted); (c) ART 356 used only as LAST RESORT after exhausting all other options — proclamation should be based on material grounds + subject to judicial review (later upheld in BOMMAI 1994); (d) GOVERNOR should be 'eminent person' NOT from ruling party, CONSULT CM before appointment — not a binding norm yet; (e) Governor's removal + short tenures curtailed; (f) INTER-STATE COUNCIL (Art 263) to be revitalised — set up 1990 under V.P. Singh; (g) Revenue distribution reformed — implemented via Finance Commissions; (h) planning decentralised (pre-GST centralisation). (2) PUNCHHI COMMISSION (2007-2010) — chaired by JUSTICE MADAN MOHAN PUNCHHI (former CJI). Set up by UPA-I. Submitted 7-volume REPORT in MARCH 2010. Went further than Sarkaria. KEY RECOMMENDATIONS: (a) FIXED 5-YEAR TERM for Governors; remove 'pleasure' doctrine; NO REMOVAL without cause (address through Presidential process); (b) panel of 5 names for CM appointment in hung assembly; (c) a process for REMOVAL of Governors (impeachment by State legislature); (d) Treaty-making power — states should have voice in matters affecting them; (e) localise some all-India service cadre; (f) give MARGINAL states more say in national decisions; (g) coordinated response to internal security issues. IMPLEMENTATION: both Commissions' recommendations only PARTIALLY implemented. Inter-State Council has met only sporadically. Governors' politicisation persists. CENTRE-STATE tensions remain (GST compensation, law + order, disaster relief, CAG audits).
